title: The Libertine
full_review:
"You will not like me," warns Johnny Depp as John Wilmot, the Restoration-era poet in the opening ribald monologue of "The Libertine" (Weinstein). And indeed, truer words were never spoken.

Which is not to disparage Depp's extravagantly over-the-top and fitfully entertaining performance, but his character is tiresomely self-destructive and licentious, and the film itself -- a dank and seamy 17th-century tale -- is slow-moving and overly enamored of the era's bawdiness for its own good.

The year is 1660, and Charles II reigns after a period of repressive Puritan rule. The arts and sciences are flourishing, and so, the film's introductory title informs us, is "sexual intercourse."

Wilmot, the real-life second Earl of Rochester, was a provocative rake whose literary output -- poems and a play -- mirrored a debauched lifestyle. He had a love-hate relationship with King Charles II (John Malkovich), with whom he fell in and out of favor. As the action begins, he has just returned from exile after some infraction.

His cronies, and sparring partners, include playwright George Etheredge (Tom Hollander), whose comedy "The Man of Mode" features a Wilmot-like personage, and wit Charles Sackville (Johnny Vegas). A young fellow named Downs (Rupert Friend) joins their coterie, and he becomes a sort of mascot for Rochester, with subtle homoerotic undertones.

Rochester is married to Elizabeth Malet (Rosamund Pike), whom he had abducted -- a crime for which he was imprisoned in the Tower of London, but was pardoned by the king -- after which, incredibly, Elizabeth wed him.

He seems to care for Elizabeth, but despite admonitions to mend his ways from his disapproving mother (Francesca Annis), he can't contain his inveterate womanizing ways, including a liaison with a prostitute (Kelly Reilly). One night at the theater, he sees inept actress Elizabeth Barry (Samantha Morton) roundly booed off the stage. He sees greatness in her, nonetheless, and resolves to groom her for stardom. In short order, he succeeds.

Meanwhile, the king commissions him to write a play that will put the English on equal footing with the visiting French, renowned for their cultural accomplishments. Rochester can't resist taking the opportunity to skewer King Charles in a tawdry piece meant to satirize the sexual extravagances at court.

Director Laurence Dunmore's adaptation of Stephen Jeffreys' play is generally well acted. Depp's high-cheekboned hauteur is put to good use here, and he gets to disintegrate into a disfigured, scabrous wreck of a man (dying at 33 of syphilis and alcohol poisoning), but it's Malkovich (who played Rochester on stage) who impresses more with his assured portrayal of the conflicted monarch. Pike, Hollander, Vegas and Friend excel in their respective parts.

Even with its somewhat redemptive ending -- a deathbed epiphany -- "The Libertine" is unpleasantly distasteful, wallowing excessively in its protagonist's unbridled lust, and with such a colorful, if reprehensible, protagonist at its center, it is surprisingly lacking in dramatic momentum.

The film contains much rough and crude language, vulgar sexual expressions and imagery, sexual situations, adultery, partial and rear nudity, a crass scene of urination, some anticlerical remarks and violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
